stops.title: A throw traces a parabola
stops.notes: Why does the ball curve even though it keeps moving forward? We will connect this picture to two equations and a Rust function.

stops.title: Ignore air resistance
stops.notes: Gravity is the only force in this ideal model. There is no horizontal acceleration.

stops.title: Gravity stays constant
stops.notes: Use g = 9.81 metres per second squared downward.

stops.title: Return to the launch height
stops.notes: The 45-degree optimum depends on equal launch and landing heights, as well as ignoring drag.

stops.title: At the apex
stops.notes: Only the vertical velocity is zero. Horizontal velocity is still about 14.1 metres per second and gravity still acts downward.

stops.title: Same clock, two equations
stops.notes: At 20 metres per second and 45 degrees, the ball returns to the ground after about 2.88 seconds and travels about 40.8 metres. The animation deliberately slows that flight down.

stops.title: Why 45 degrees?
stops.notes: Solve y(T) = 0 for T = 2 v0 sin(theta) / g, then substitute into x(T). Range is v0 squared times sin(2 theta), divided by g. Sine is maximised when 2 theta is 90 degrees. The 30- and 60-degree throws have equal range, but different heights and flight times; these curves draw by fraction of each flight.

stops.title: Turn the equations into Rust
stops.notes: vx and vy are the launch velocity components in metres per second; t is seconds. Screen y increases downward, so draw at ground_y minus scale times y. Stop at the flight time rather than drawing underground.

stops.title: One clock
stops.notes: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent, but evaluated at the same time.

stops.title: A parabola
stops.notes: Eliminating time between a linear x(t) and quadratic y(t) produces a parabola.

stops.title: Know the assumptions
stops.notes: Ask: do 30 and 60 degrees have the same flight time? No. Then ask what happens to the 45-degree result if drag matters or landing height changes.
